title: FDEs: Building Capacity, Not Dependency | Cohere
gist: Cohere argues the enterprise AI bottleneck has moved from experimentation to production deployment, and positions its forward-deployed engineers (FDEs) as a way to close that gap while explicitly designing against the vendor lock-in risk that close-in deployment support usually creates.

insights.claim: The main constraint on enterprise AI adoption has shifted from proving AI works in pilots to adapting it to real-world production operating environments.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: Vendors and service providers whose value proposition is production deployment support (not just model quality) should see rising demand; investors should weight enterprise AI vendors' deployment/services capability, not just benchmark scores.
insights.quote: The main bottleneck in enterprise AI adoption has shifted downstream from experimentation to production deployment.

insights.claim: Per Deloitte's 2026 State of AI in the Enterprise report, only 25% of organizations have moved 40% or more of their AI pilots into production.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: A concrete, citable stat quantifying the pilot-to-production gap in enterprise AI — useful as a benchmark for tracking enterprise AI adoption momentum over coming quarters.
insights.quote: According to Deloitte’s 2026 State of AI in the Enterprise report, only 25% of organizations have moved 40% or more of their AI pilots into production.

insights.claim: Enterprises facing the deployment gap have several options: build internal AI deployment expertise, hire IT consultancies or specialist AI firms, use independent contractors, use model-aligned service providers, or use the model vendor's own forward-deployed engineers.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: Maps the competitive landscape for enterprise AI deployment spend — consultancies (Accenture, Deloitte-type firms), boutique AI shops, and model vendors' internal FDE teams are all competing for the same budget line.

themes.theme: Vendor FDEs vs third-party service providers

insights.claim: Cohere argues its vendor-employed forward-deployed engineers have a structural advantage over third-party consultancies because they combine hands-on customer deployment work with direct access to Cohere's research and engineering teams and to the underlying model code.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: Model vendors that also sell deployment services (FDE model) can differentiate from pure consultancies by offering faster root-cause fixes; watch whether OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google follow similar FDE-as-a-service go-to-market moves for enterprise accounts.
insights.quote: Vendor FDEs occupy a unique position: they work hands-on within the customer’s technical and operating environment while remaining part of the company building the underlying AI technology.
insights.locator: What FDEs offer that third-party services can’t easily replicate

insights.claim: When a customer use case exposes a gap in Cohere's product, Cohere's FDEs can inspect or modify the underlying code with core engineering to build a fix that is later generalized across all customers.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: Suggests Cohere's product roadmap is partly customer-deployment-driven rather than purely research-driven — a source of incremental product improvement and customer lock-in via co-developed features.
insights.locator: What FDEs offer that third-party services can’t easily replicate

insights.claim: Third-party providers bring broader industry expertise and vendor-neutral independence, but have less visibility into root causes of product limitations or model behavior and often resort to bespoke workarounds or escalate back to the vendor, adding complexity and maintenance burden.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: A vendor-authored critique of the consultancy/systems-integrator model for AI deployment — useful context when evaluating claims from Accenture-style AI transformation practices versus vendor-native delivery teams.
insights.locator: What FDEs offer that third-party services can’t easily replicate

insights.claim: A Cohere customer's meeting-briefing agent kept failing because its instructions referenced non-existent tools and its tool calls couldn't handle the required context; Cohere's FDE rebuilt the agent and modified supporting tools, including its Slack integration, to handle larger context.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: Illustrates a real, concrete failure mode of agentic AI in production (broken tool references, context-window limits on tool calls) that other enterprises deploying agents should proactively test for.
insights.quote: The agent was failing frequently because its instructions referenced tools that didn’t exist, while some of the underlying tool calls couldn’t handle the required context.
insights.locator: For example, one Cohere customer had built an agent...

insights.claim: The FDE advantage is not just faster escalation of problems, but a wider set of options for making a deployment work without having to engineer workarounds around the product's limitations.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: Frames the FDE model's competitive moat as root-cause access rather than speed alone, a distinction worth testing against customer references before crediting the claim.
insights.quote: The FDE advantage isn’t simply faster escalation; it’s a wider set of options for getting the deployment to work without defaulting to engineering around the product.

insights.claim: Cohere distinguishes two types of lock-in from AI vendor relationships: commercial/architectural dependency inherent to choosing a given vendor's models, APIs, or platform (which exists regardless of who deploys it), and operational dependency, where critical system knowledge stays with the vendor's engineers rather than the customer's own team.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: A reusable due-diligence framework for enterprises (and investors assessing enterprise AI vendor stickiness/switching costs) to separate unavoidable platform lock-in from avoidable operational lock-in when evaluating vendor contracts.
insights.quote: The more FDE-specific lock-in risk is operational dependency.
insights.locator: The core concern: Do FDEs create vendor lock-in?

insights.claim: If operational knowledge of an AI deployment remains concentrated with the vendor's FDEs, the enterprise customer ends up owning the deployment but not the capability to operate it, which increases exposure to the vendor's pricing, product direction, and commercial terms over time.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: A candid articulation of the switching-cost mechanism that makes AI vendors' service-heavy deployments commercially sticky — relevant to modeling net-revenue-retention and pricing power for AI infrastructure vendors.
insights.quote: In other words, the enterprise may end up owning the deployment but not the capability to operate it.
insights.locator: The core concern: Do FDEs create vendor lock-in?

insights.claim: Cohere positions knowledge transfer as a core part of its FDE delivery model from the outset rather than a handover step at project end, arguing this determines whether operational dependency becomes a permanent feature of the engagement.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: A go-to-market and retention narrative aimed at enterprise buyers wary of lock-in; investors should treat this as a claim to verify via customer churn/expansion data rather than take at face value.
insights.quote: It largely depends on whether the vendor builds knowledge transfer into the delivery model from the outset rather than treating it as a handover exercise at the end.
insights.locator: Building customer capability into the FDE approach

insights.claim: Cohere's FDEs run customer enablement sessions for major features and train internal 'champions' who then teach and support other teams across the customer's organization, including technical sessions on Model Context Protocol (MCP) implementation patterns.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: Confirms Cohere is actively standardizing enterprise customers on MCP for tool/agent integration, aligning with broader industry adoption of MCP as the agentic-tooling interoperability layer.
insights.locator: Building customer capability into the FDE approach

insights.claim: Cohere's FDEs help customers build reusable engineering practices around deployment, load testing, and connector development, and build test suites tied to core product functionality so internal teams can independently verify system behavior as models, integrations, and configurations change.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: Signals a maturing enterprise-AI ops discipline (testing/evaluation infrastructure for agentic systems) that is becoming a standard deliverable, not an afterthought — relevant for AI observability/eval tooling vendors as a complementary or competing capability.
insights.locator: Capability-building also extends beyond knowledge of the system itself

insights.claim: Cohere states its ultimate FDE goal is not just transferring knowledge of the current deployment but giving customers the ongoing ability to operate, evaluate, troubleshoot, and extend their AI system independently.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: The stated end-state metric enterprise buyers can hold Cohere to when negotiating FDE engagement scope and success criteria.
insights.quote: Our ultimate goal is not only to transfer knowledge about the current deployment, but to give our customers the ongoing ability to operate, evaluate, troubleshoot, and extend the AI system independently.
insights.locator: Building customer capability into the FDE approach

insights.claim: Cohere concludes that close vendor involvement in deployment should ultimately increase, not decrease, a customer's operational independence, and recommends enterprises evaluate FDE engagements on what dependency they leave behind, not just on speed to production.
insights.speaker: @cohere
insights.so_what: A buyer-side evaluation criterion investors/analysts covering enterprise AI vendors can use to assess service quality claims: ask reference customers whether internal teams can now operate the system without vendor engineers.
insights.quote: Ultimately, close vendor involvement should create greater operational independence, not less.
